newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire protesters defy ban, troops surround campus.
newsitem.headline: Zaire protesters defy ban, troops surround campus.

text.p: Hundreds of Zaireans set up roadblocks and hijacked cars in the Zaire capital on Tuesday in defiance of a government ban on anti-Rwanda demonstrations.

Witnesses said troops surrounded the university campus in the city centre, hotbed of militant students who led violent protests last week against Rwanda's alleged backing of ethnic Tutsi rebels battling the Zaire army.
Between 300 and 500 people turned up in the city centre and there were protests elsewhere in town, witnesses said.
"They threw stones at the car and tried to steal it. I just drove very fast," said a taxi driver in central Kinshasa.
Zaire on Monday banned demonstrations and authorised troops to open fire on anyone caught looting or engaging in vandalism.

A statement issued after a special cabinet meeting said the measures had become necessary because of attacks on Rwandans and Burundians in Zaire following a Tutsi revolt in the east. Zaire accuses Rwandan troops of fighting alongside the rebels.

Protesters, notably students, appeared to view the ban as intended to protect part-Tutsi Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo, who is accused of being soft on the rebellion. Marchers demanded his sacking last week and attacked Tutsi homes and property.
"We will increase pressure until Kengo leaves. A Rwandan Prime Minister cannot fight a war against Rwanda," said student activist Pierre Wadi.
Several hundred students gathered inside the campus as police arrived. There was no incident as police took up positions around the campus.
Hundreds of Tutsis hounded in anger after ethnic Tutsi rebels wrested control of Zaire's two eastern provinces were trying to flee the capital, witnesses said.
A boatload of 70 Tutsis was able to cross the river Zaire into Brazzaville, the capital of neighbouring Congo on the other bank. An equal number was waiting to cross in another boat.
A Tutsi woman who arrived in Brazzaville said by telephone some Zairean passengers threatened to throw the Tutsis into the water.
"On the baot some Zaireans said they would throw us into the water and kill us, but other Zaireans prevented them from doing so," said the woman who asked not to be named.
Some Tutsis said they paid up to $3,000 a head to cross in dugout canoes. About 400 crossed in such canoes on Monday.
The government statement on the ban on demonstrations stressed the need to avoid xenophobia in the face of what Zaire has termed aggression by Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda.
"Our country having been unjustly attacked by these two countries (Rwanda and Burundi), it is understandable that our people should feel xenophobic sentiments," the statement said.

Zaire rejected an invitation to attend regional talks in Kenya on the conflict, which has displaced hundreds of thousands of Hutu refugees from Rwanda and Burundi sheltering in eastern Zaire camps for more than two years.
